query: Earlier empirical-potential and first-principles studies primarily targeted phase-transition temperature, while other fusion properties remain difficult because they require free energies on both sides of the transition with vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling retained. Explicit ab initio free-energy evaluation is highly accurate but depends on costly molecular dynamics. TOR-TILD increased throughput for elemental and binary systems, yet slows substantially for multicomponent high-entropy systems. Under the constraint that the free energies of both solid and fluid states and the relevant entropy terms remain faithful, what single testable methodological hypothesis could substantially reduce the cost of obtaining fusion and high-temperature thermodynamic properties? State the proposed intervention and why it should work, predict its speed and fidelity relative to explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics workflows and TOR-TILD, define composition and temperature boundaries, cite supporting evidence from prior elemental or binary results, and specify a decisive benchmark of phase free energies and derived observables that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: An active‐learning machine‐learning interatomic potential framework that is coupled with enhanced sampling (e.g., umbrella integration) can reproduce accurate free energies (including vibrational, anharmonic, and electron–vibration contributions) of both solid and fluid states near fusion conditions at a fraction of the computational cost of full AIMD or TOR-TILD methods. This is achieved by selectively learning the key anharmonic configurations that mediate vibrational and electron–vibration coupling effects.
generation.material_initial_state: Elemental and binary systems (e.g., FCC Al, BCC Na) as benchmarks, with the framework later extended to multicomponent and high-entropy alloys where full AIMD and TOR-TILD become prohibitively expensive.
generation.intervention: Develop and deploy an ML potential (e.g., deep potential or moment tensor potential) using active learning to refine the training set on-the-fly, combined with enhanced free-energy sampling techniques (such as umbrella integration with Gaussian Process Regression for uncertainty quantification) to capture the complete free energy surface.
generation.conditions: The method is applied over a temperature range from well below to above the melting (fusion) points, under conditions where both electronic and vibrational entropy contributions are significant, and for systems without extreme anharmonicity beyond what the training ensemble can capture.
generation.structural_mediator: The accurate capture of atomic displacement covariances (vibrational entropy) and anharmonic interactions, which are encoded in the ML potential through active sampling of key configurational states.
generation.mechanism: By training on a limited but representative set of configurations that include both harmonic and anharmonic regimes, the ML potential learns to reproduce the force landscape and associated free energy contributions. Enhanced sampling (via umbrella integration) then efficiently reconstructs the full free-energy profile for both solid and liquid states, minimizing the need for extensive AIMD trajectories while retaining fidelity to the underlying physics.
generation.predicted_outcome: The ML-based framework will predict phase free energies and fusion properties (such as melting temperature and latent heat) within experimental or high-level AIMD error bounds, while reducing computational time by approximately an order of magnitude relative to full AIMD and TOR-TILD approaches.
generation.baseline: Explicit ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) free-energy calculations and TOR-TILD methods that require extensive sampling of atomic configurations.
generation.boundary: Valid for elemental and binary systems as demonstrated benchmarks, with applicability to multicomponent high-entropy alloys subject to adequate active learning coverage of unexpected anharmonic regions; caution remains for systems where cooperative or complex anharmonic effects (beyond Gaussian covariances) dominate.
generation.uncertainty: While preliminary studies in elemental and binary systems support the approach, the exact computational speed-up and fidelity in highly multicomponent systems have not been fully quantified and remain subject to further testing.

falsification_experiment.design: Select a set of benchmark systems (e.g., FCC Al, BCC Na, and a representative binary alloy) for which high-fidelity AIMD-based free energy surfaces are available. Develop the ML potential using active learning with umbrella integration to compute the free energies in both the solid and liquid phases over a temperature range covering the fusion transition. Compare predicted melting temperatures, latent heats, and absolute free energy differences against those from full AIMD calculations and experimental measurements.
measurements: Absolute free energy differences between phases
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ML-enhanced free energy method produces phase free energies or derived observables (e.g., melting temperature, latent heat) that deviate by more than an acceptable error margin (e.g., >5% relative error) from AIMD/experimental benchmarks, or if computational savings are less than a factor of ~5–10, then the hypothesis is falsified.

We employ the general framework of machine-learning (ML)-based approaches, which have emerged recently as a systematic framework to develop potentials with accuracies near that of the underlying DFT calculations for elemental and multicomponent systems,. Here, using training data reported previously for elemental, binary, ternary, and quaternary systems in Nb–Ta–Mo–W, we developed a potential for the MoNbTaW RHEA based on the moment tensor potential (MTP) formalism, which has been found to feature an excellent balance between accuracy and computational cost. The flowchart for constructing the MTP is shown in Fig. 1a with the methodological details provided in “Methods”. The basic materials property predictions of the MTP model are provided in Supplementary Table 1. Figure 1b, c shows a comparison of the DFT- and MTP-predicted energies and forces for both training and test sets. AbstractThe vibrational entropy of a solid at finite temperature is investigated from the perspective of information theory. Ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) simulations generate ensembles of atomic configurations at finite temperature from which we obtain the N-body distribution of atomic displacements, ρN. We calculate the information-theoretic entropy from the expectation value of lnρN. At a first level of approximation, treating individual atomic displacements independently, our method may be applied using Debye–Waller B-factors, allowing diffraction experiments to obtain an upper bound on the thermodynamic entropy. At the next level of approximation we correct the overestimation through inclusion of displacement covariances. We apply this approach to elemental body-centered cubic sodium and face-centered cubic aluminum, showing good agreement with experimental values above the Debye temperatures of the metals. Below the Debye temperatures, we extract an effective vibrational density of states from eigenvalues of the covariance matrix, and then evaluate the entropy quantum mechanically, again yielding good agreement with experiment down to low temperatures. We use the Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package (VASP []) using augmented plane wave potentials [] with the Perdew–Burke–Ernzerhof (PBE []) generalized gradient exchange correlation functional. We use a single electronic k-point and default plane wave energy cutoffs. When possible we use experimental lattice constants at the appropriate temperatures. The molecular dynamics simulations use Nosé thermostats with the default Nosé mass parameters. Our time steps are 2 fs, and our runs extend to 40 ps for Al (4×4×4) and 8 ps for (6×6×6), and 7 ps or greater for Na.
